title: United States v. Gayle (2d Cir. 2003) — Ingram’s foreign predicate conviction
shortTitle: United States v. Gayle (2d Cir. 2003) — Ingram’s foreign predicate conviction
summary: The Second Circuit read the felon-in-possession provision’s reference to conviction in any court as limited to domestic convictions.
notes: The Supreme Court later adopted the same domestic-only reading of 'convicted in any court' in Small v. United States (2005).

sections.Parties: The appeal involved Rohan Ingram, a codefendant with Kirk Gayle and Ann-Marie Richardson, and the United States. Katzmann’s discussion concerns Ingram’s felon-in-possession count.
sections.Material Facts: Authorities arrested Ingram at a Plattsburgh hotel on suspicion of illegal entry from Canada and found firearms in his room. A jury convicted him of two conspiracy counts and being a felon in possession. The predicate for the possession charge was a 1996 Canadian conviction for using a firearm in an indictable offense. Section 922(g)(1) applied to a person convicted in any court of a crime punishable by imprisonment exceeding one year. The issue was the foreign location of the prior conviction, not its length-of-punishment threshold.
sections.Procedural History: Ingram moved to dismiss the possession count on the ground that his Canadian conviction did not qualify. The district judge treated any court as unambiguously including foreign courts. On appeal, the Second Circuit rejected that reading and concluded that the Canadian conviction could not serve as the predicate. Katzmann’s narrative does not provide the complete formal mandate or disposition of the other counts.
sections.Issue: Did conviction in any court include a conviction entered by a foreign court?
sections.Holding: The panel held that the statutory phrase included domestic convictions only, excluding Ingram’s Canadian conviction.
sections.Reasoning: The panel found competing plausible readings. The gun-safety purpose could favor foreign violent-crime predicates, but unlimited inclusion could import convictions for conduct protected or treated less severely here and convictions produced by incompatible procedures. Section 921’s exception for federal or state business-regulation offenses would also yield different treatment of equivalent foreign offenses if the general prohibition were worldwide. The panel then examined the Senate report’s domestic definition of felony and the conference report’s adoption of punishment-based language without a stated change in geographic scope. It regarded those materials as evidence against inclusion. Congress could choose broader coverage by speaking more clearly. The analysis should not confuse a predicate element of the possession offense with a generic sentence enhancement; Katzmann also discusses a separate circuit’s enhancement context.

topics.lrs-k-textualism: The panel found that the word any did not resolve the geographic class of courts.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: Senate and conference reports helped the panel resolve the geographic ambiguity.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The domestic business-offense exceptions created a contextual problem for the broader reading.
topics.lrs-k-domestic-assumption: Gayle is the Second Circuit's reading of 'convicted in any court' as domestic only, the exact question this concept covers.
topics.lrs-k-gun-predicate: The predicate-conviction language of § 922(g)(1) (and the § 921(a)(20) definition) is the statute Gayle construes.
